sections.body:
# Defenses & Mitigations

Now that you've seen the attacks across this module, it's time to build the defenses. There's one core idea that everything else in this lesson builds on:

**You cannot make the LLM itself trustworthy, so you must make its actions safe instead.**

In other words, don't try to build a model that can never be tricked — that's an unsolved problem, and probably always will be to some degree. Instead, assume the model *will* get tricked at some point, and design the system around it so that even a fully manipulated model cannot cause serious harm.

- *Analogy:* You don't design a bank vault assuming the security guard can never be fooled or bribed. You design it so that even if the guard *is* fooled, the vault door still needs a second key, cameras are still recording, and an alarm still goes off. The guard being tricked is not the end of the story — it's just the first layer failing.

## The Defense-in-Depth Model

Good agent security uses many layers stacked on top of each other, the same way a castle isn't protected by just one wall — it has a moat, then a wall, then guards, then a locked inner keep. If an attacker gets past one layer, the next one is still there waiting. This approach is called **defense in depth**, and it's the backbone of everything in this lesson.

sections.body:
## Layer 1: Least Privilege (the Most Important Layer)

Give every tool, and every agent, the **absolute minimum** access it needs to do its job — nothing more. If a support agent only ever needs to look up *one* customer's orders at a time, its database tool should be physically incapable of reading anyone else's data, not just "instructed" not to.

- *Analogy:* A hotel keycard opens exactly one room, not the whole building — even if someone steals it, the damage is limited to one room, not every guest's belongings.

Practical rules:

- Scope every tool call to the *current user only* — never let it query "any" record by ID with no ownership check.
- Give read-only tools wherever a write isn't actually needed.
- Keep high-risk tools (payments, deletions, external emails) in a separate agent that never directly sees untrusted input like documents or web pages.

## Layer 2: Human in the Loop

For high-impact actions — sending money, deleting data, emailing people outside the company — require an actual human to approve before it happens. The agent can *propose* the action, but a person has to *confirm* it.

- *Analogy:* A junior employee can draft a wire transfer, but it still needs a manager's signature before the money actually moves. The junior employee being tricked into drafting a bad transfer doesn't matter if the manager catches it.

This single control neutralizes most of the worst-case attacks in this entire module, because even a fully tricked agent still can't *complete* the damaging action all on its own — it can only ask.

## Layer 3: Sandboxing and Isolation

Run risky operations — running code, parsing documents, browsing the web — inside an isolated environment that has nothing valuable in it:

- No access to secrets, passwords, or API keys.
- No network access at all, or only a short allowlist of approved destinations.
- Limited CPU, memory, and execution time, so nothing can run forever or overload the system.
- A disposable container that gets destroyed completely after each use.

- *Analogy:* Think of it like a hotel's guest Wi-Fi network, kept completely separate from the hotel's internal staff network. Even if someone breaks into the guest Wi-Fi, there's simply nothing important reachable from there.

If an attacker somehow escapes into the sandbox, they find nothing worth stealing, and nowhere further to go.

## Layer 4: Input and Context Handling

- **Fence untrusted content** clearly as data, not as instructions — the same `<DATA>` tagging idea from the document chaining lesson.
- **Strip dangerous tools** out of the agent's available toolset entirely while it's processing untrusted input, so even a successful injection has nothing dangerous to call.
- **Validate every tool input in code** — check types, ranges, and formats, rather than trusting the model to only ever send reasonable values.
- **Never put secrets** (API keys, passwords, internal tokens) anywhere the model can see them — not in the prompt, and not in any tool output the model reads back.

## Layer 5: Output and Action Controls

- **Validate and encode output** before it's used anywhere else — this prevents an LLM's own output from becoming an XSS or SQL injection attack on a downstream system (covered in detail in the LLM Output Attacks module).
- **Rate-limit tool calls** to stop a manipulated agent from looping forever, or exfiltrating data in bulk before anyone notices.
- **Constrain tool inputs to a fixed set of allowed values** wherever possible, instead of accepting free-form text — for example, a `status` field should only ever accept `"approved"` or `"rejected"`, never an arbitrary string.

## Layer 6: Automated Guardrails (Classifiers)

Everything so far relies on hard rules written in code — a tool either has access or it doesn't, a value either matches an allowed list or it's rejected. But some attacks are fuzzy and don't fit a clean rule: a cleverly worded jailbreak, a document with a subtly hidden instruction, a response that's *technically* valid but clearly manipulated. For these, many production systems add one more layer: a small, fast **classifier model** whose only job is to scan text and flag it as suspicious — separate from the main LLM doing the actual work.

This usually runs in two places:

- **On the way in:** scanning untrusted input (documents, web pages, tool results) for known prompt-injection patterns before the main agent ever reads them.
- **On the way out:** scanning the agent's proposed action or response for policy violations (e.g. leaking a secret, recommending a malicious link) before it's actually executed or shown to the user.

- *Analogy:* This is like an airport metal detector in addition to security guards. The guards (your code-level rules) handle the well-defined threats. The detector (the classifier) catches things that look wrong even when no single rule technically flags them.

**Important limitation:** a guardrail classifier is a probabilistic filter, not a guarantee — it reduces risk, it doesn't eliminate it. It should sit *alongside* the hard, code-level rules from Layers 1–5, never replace them.

# Rate limiting: stops a manipulated agent from looping or mass-exfiltrating,
# even if it has been tricked into trying.

import time

call_log = {}  # user_id -> list of call timestamps

def rate_limited(user_id, max_calls=10, window_seconds=60):
    now = time.time()
    calls = call_log.setdefault(user_id, [])
    # Keep only calls from within the current time window
    calls[:] = [t for t in calls if now - t < window_seconds]
    if len(calls) >= max_calls:
        return True  # blocked
    calls.append(now)
    return False

def send_email_tool(user_id, to_address, body):
    if rate_limited(user_id):
        raise RuntimeError("Rate limit reached — too many email sends recently")
    # ... actually send the email only if not rate limited


# Logging and monitoring: every sensitive action is recorded, so unusual
# behavior can be caught even if it wasn't blocked in the moment.

def log_action(action, target, user_id, details=None):
    print(f"[AUDIT] user={user_id} action={action} target={target} details={details}")
    # In a real system: send this to a monitoring system that can alert on
    # patterns like "one user triggered 200 refunds in a minute."

**Design principle:** security lives in the *tools and the surrounding code (the orchestrator)*, not in the prompt. A rule written in the system prompt is just a suggestion — a clever enough attacker can often talk the model out of following it. A check written in actual code is a wall the model has no way to climb over, no matter how it's been tricked. Guardrail classifiers add a useful extra layer, but they sit on top of this code-level foundation, not in place of it.

## Vulnerable vs Secure Agent, Side by Side

| Aspect | Vulnerable | Secure |
|--------|------------|--------|
| Tool scope | Broad, all data reachable | Scoped to the current user only |
| Secrets | In the prompt / visible in tool output | Never visible to the model at all |
| Risky actions | Auto-executed immediately | Human approval required first |
| Untrusted input | Mixed in with real instructions | Clearly fenced, dangerous tools stripped away |
| Suspicious content | Only caught if a hard rule happens to match | Also flagged by a guardrail classifier |
| Code execution | Runs on the main host | Isolated, disposable sandbox |
| Visibility | No logs at all | Every sensitive action fully logged |

## Defenses Are Not "Set and Forget"

Attackers adapt, and a defense that works today may not work against a new technique next month. Treat this checklist as a starting baseline, not a finish line:

- **Test your own defenses on purpose.** Regularly try known attack patterns from this module against your own agent, in a safe test environment, to confirm the controls actually hold up in practice — not just on paper.
- **Revisit after any new attack technique becomes public.** If a new prompt-injection or evasion method appears in research or the news, check whether your existing layers would catch it.
- **Use structured threat modeling** (covered in the Threat Modeling module) to keep track of what's protected, what's assumed, and what's still an open risk — rather than relying on memory of "what we fixed last time."

## Key Takeaways

- Assume the model *will* be tricked at some point — the goal is making sure that doesn't matter, not making that impossible.
- Least privilege is the single strongest control: limit what each tool and agent can even reach in the first place.
- Human approval turns a "catastrophic automatic action" into "just a request that a person can reject."
- Sandboxing means even a successful escape finds nothing valuable and nowhere to go.
- Automated guardrail classifiers catch fuzzy, rule-defying attacks that hard-coded checks miss — but they're a probabilistic extra layer, not a replacement for code-level controls.
- Rate limiting and logging don't prevent an attack outright, but they limit the damage and make it visible after the fact.
- Defenses need to be tested and revisited regularly — a control that worked yesterday isn't guaranteed to work against tomorrow's attack technique.
- The golden rule: enforce security in code (the tools and orchestrator), never rely on the prompt alone — a prompt is a suggestion, code is a wall.
